title: Quality expectations and cost-based competition

match.reason: No existing point covers how operations balance customer quality expectations against price competition; the closest, customers, suppliers and competitors, is a broader Year 11 idea about market forces rather than this operations trade-off.

draft.title: Quality expectations and cost-based competition
card: Customers expect goods and services to work well, last and match what was promised. A business that falls short can lose sales and its reputation.
Rivals may cut their prices to win customers. To match them, a business needs lower costs, so it can charge less and still make a profit.
The two pull against each other. Cheaper materials, fewer checks or faster production can cut costs, but they can also lower quality.
Operations managers must balance the two. They look for savings that keep quality at the level customers expect, such as less waste or better scheduling.
draft.remember: Operations must keep costs low enough to compete on price without letting quality fall below what customers expect.

a.q: Why is cost-based competition a challenge for a business that also wants to keep its quality high?
opts: Cutting costs can lower quality, which customers notice
Higher quality always means a lower price for customers
Customers stop expecting good quality when prices fall
Rivals who cut prices must also raise their quality
a.why: To match lower prices, a business must cut costs, and some cuts, such as cheaper materials, can lower quality. Customers still expect good quality, so the business must balance the two. Quality does not automatically fall when prices do, but the pressure is there.
a.clue: Think about what a business might do to lower its costs.

b.q: A bakery chain in Newcastle faces a rival selling bread at a lower price. Which response best balances cost and quality?
opts: Cut waste by baking to demand, and keep the same recipe
Switch to a cheaper flour that makes the bread go stale
Stop checking loaves before they leave the bakery
Ignore the rival and raise prices to show quality
b.why: Baking to demand cuts waste and cost while the bread stays the same quality. Cheaper flour that makes bread go stale and skipping checks both save money but lower quality that customers expect. Raising prices ignores the cost pressure from the rival.
b.clue: Look for the option that saves money without changing what the customer gets.

a.best: Cutting costs can lower quality, which customers notice

b.best: Cut waste by baking to demand, and keep the same recipe

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('can'). The distractors all use absolute or sweeping claims ('stop expecting', 'always', 'must'), so a student could pick it from the wording alone without knowing the idea.
